opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the adversarial examples phenomenon tells us something quite important about how our current systems work, and also about how they differ from human vision.

If you look at a typical convolutional network or a transformer trained for classification, it's essentially a feedforward, bottom-up pipeline. Pixels come in, you compute features layer by layer, and at the end you get a label. The decision is made in one sweep. And what adversarial examples show is that you can make tiny, imperceptible perturbations to the pixels, carefully chosen, and push the representation across a decision boundary. The network says "ostrich" when it's clearly a school bus.

Now, human vision is not like that. We have strong bottom-up processing, of course: edges, textures, grouping, figure-ground. But we also have a great deal of top-down processing. There are massive feedback connections in the visual cortex, often more feedback than feedforward. When you perceive an object, you're not just pattern-matching on local features. You have a hypothesis: "this is a car." That hypothesis makes predictions. A car has wheels in certain places, windows, a certain 3D shape, it sits on the ground, it casts a shadow. You can check whether the image is consistent with that interpretation.

So the idea is a kind of analysis by synthesis, an old idea in vision going back decades. You go bottom-up to generate candidate hypotheses, then top-down to verify them. If someone has perturbed a few pixels so the bottom-up system shouts "ostrich," the top-down check asks: where's the long neck? Where are the legs? Is there anything ostrich-like in the 3D structure? None of that is there. The hypothesis fails verification and you reject it.

What makes this robust is that the adversary now has to fool two quite different processes at once. Fooling a local feature detector with a small perturbation is easy. Fooling a system that demands global consistency — shape, parts, geometry, context — while keeping the perturbation imperceptible is much harder, because you'd essentially have to change the image so it actually looks like an ostrich.

I'd also connect this to grounding vision in the 3D world. A lot of my work over the years has argued that we should recover shape, depth, and parts, not just labels. Those structured representations give the top-down process something meaningful to check against. A purely 2D statistical classifier has no such anchor.

I wouldn't claim this is a complete solution. It's still an open research problem, and building top-down verification into modern deep networks in a scalable way isn't trivial. But I do think the path to robustness looks less like patching a feedforward classifier and more like building vision systems that perceive the way biological systems do, with an iterative interplay between data-driven evidence and model-driven expectation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think adversarial examples tell us something quite deep about the current paradigm, which is that these networks are essentially doing bottom-up pattern recognition. You take pixels, you pass them through a sequence of filters and nonlinearities, and at the end you read off a label. The problem is that the mapping from pixels to labels is being learned purely statistically, and so there can be these very peculiar directions in pixel space where a tiny perturbation, imperceptible to a human, pushes you across a decision boundary. The network has no notion that what it's looking at is still a panda, because it has no model of what a panda is beyond the correlations it has picked up.

Now, if you look at how biological vision works, and this goes back to work from the 1970s and 1980s, there is a great deal of top-down processing. The feedforward sweep gets you a quick first guess, but then there are these recurrent, feedback connections, and the hypothesis is tested against the evidence. You form a hypothesis about what the object is, and that hypothesis makes predictions, about its shape, its parts, how it would look under a slightly different viewpoint or illumination, and you check whether the image is consistent with those predictions. That is analysis by synthesis, an idea that people like Grenander and later Mumford articulated very clearly.

So why would that help with adversarial examples? Because an adversarial perturbation fools the classifier, but it doesn't change the actual geometry or structure of the scene. If I have a hypothesis that this is a gibbon, I should be able to ask, where is the face, where are the limbs, is the segmentation consistent with a gibbon shape, does this region look like fur? And the perturbed panda image will fail all of those tests. The bottom-up signal says gibbon, but the top-down verification says no, the parts aren't there, the evidence doesn't support it. A system that requires agreement between the two is going to be much harder to fool, because now the attacker has to construct an image that is consistent with the hypothesis at every level, not just at the final layer, and that is essentially the same as making it actually look like a gibbon.

I'll say one more thing. I think a lot of the robustness in human vision comes from the fact that we are not really doing classification, we are doing perception in service of action. We perceive objects as things in a three-dimensional world that we can interact with, and those geometric and physical constraints are very hard to spoof. So my view is that the way out is not more data or bigger networks alone, it's architectures that have these generative, hypothesis-driven components and that reason about the world, not just about labels. That's a harder research program, but I think it's the right one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses top-down feedback and hypothesis testing in vision, but does not explain dreaming as concepts activating the visual cortex.

r002.rationale: It links top-down, hypothesis-driven image understanding to generative components and analysis by synthesis, where hypotheses predict visual evidence that is checked against the image.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the problem is that our recognition systems can give you an answer without having to explain the image. They take the pixels, do a sequence of computations, and say, “This is a dog.” But we can ask a further question: if this is a dog, where is its head? Where are its legs? Do those parts fit together in a plausible way?

The bottom-up process gives you candidate interpretations. The top-down process then says, “If this interpretation is correct, here is what I should expect to find,” and checks that against the image. That creates an opportunity to reject an answer that is supported by some misleading cues but isn't consistent with the overall structure.

Now, I wouldn't claim that this automatically solves adversarial examples. You could attack that whole system too. But I think requiring an interpretation to explain the evidence, rather than simply produce a category label, is an important direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the problem is that our current recognition systems make a very rapid, bottom-up decision. You take the pixels, pass them through a sequence of layers, and out comes a label. But there is no real check that the interpretation makes sense in terms of the structure of the image.

A top-down process could ask: If this is a dog, where are the parts? How are they arranged? Can I explain the contours and the regions that I actually see? The bottom-up process proposes an interpretation, and the top-down process checks it against the evidence.

Now, I wouldn’t claim that this automatically solves adversarial examples. You can potentially attack that whole system as well. But it gives us a richer notion of recognition: not simply assigning a category, but finding an interpretation that accounts for the image. I think that is a promising direction for making these systems more robust.
